newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerian president returns to poll in fresh gamble.
newsitem.headline: Algerian president returns to poll in fresh gamble.

text.p: Algerian President Liamine Zeroual for the second time in a year is gambling on the ballot box to show that his violence-ridden North African country is pulling out of crisis.

Diplomats and analysts in the Algerian capital said on Tuesday that Zeroual's announcement of a November 28 referendum to change the constitution showed the former general was set on pushing ahead with his reform programme.
But, they say, crucial to the ballot will be the turnout and whether the security forces can provide a shield for the near 13-million electorate to go to the poll.
"The level of turnout will be a major test, and if security can be provided," said one Western diplomat.
Underlining his words on security was a statement from the security forces that the manager of Algeria's mass-circulation Echourouk newspaper was shot dead as he left home on Tuesday.
And just hours after Zeroual spoke, a bomb killed three people and wounded 13 in the northern town of Lakhdaria.
"Two weeks ago, according to the best figures available, the death toll in the conflict was running at between 100 and 150 a week," the diplomat said.
An estimated 50,000 people have been killed in violence which erupted after the authorities in January 1992 cancelled a general election in which Islamists had taken a strong lead.

Zeroual has said that "residual terrorism" remained but was on the way to being eliminated. In what was widely seen as a sign of his confidence at home, the president on Tuesday left for an extended trip to Gulf states, China and Vietnam.
In his speech on Monday, Zeroual said: "It is an absolute necessity for Algeria to bring together all the necessary conditions to avoid returning again...to the same trials."

The changes suggested to the constitution include banning political parties based on religion and confirm that Islam is Algeria's state religion. They also propose a second house of parliament, a Council of State to oversee administration and a High Court of State to try any president failing to respect the law or who "betrays the people's confidence".
Officials have long said that the now-outlawed Islamic Salvation Front (FIS), which dominated the earlier election, had hijacked religion as a political weapon.

Poverty, perceived high level corruption, and lack of hope for the future, in a nation with more than two million of its five million workforce jobless, were also seen as forces driving disenchanted young people to the fundamentalists.

Economic analysts said they believed Zeroual was gambling on being able to stick to his timetable, which will lead to promised general elections in the first half of 1997, with the aim of showing that Algeria was returning to normal and was a safe haven for investment and foreign loans.
"When the government has said it will do something, under Zeroual, within a particular timescale it has stuck to it," one analyst said.
A diplomat commented: "Zeroual is a strong individual. He has shown he is determined to go ahead with his programme."

Zeroual went to the polls last November in Algeria's first multi-candidate presidential election. He was already in power, appointed by the military authorities in January 1994, but had no mandate from the country's 29 million people.
He won with more than seven million votes. Sheikh Mahfoud Nahnah of the legal Hamas Islamist party came second with more than two million.
In the face of Moslem guerrilla threats to disrupt the poll and kill voters, the authorities deployed more than 200,000 security force members.

Zeroual said on Monday: "We must not forget today that gaps in our constitutional order enabled interests...both internal and external, to try to strike our national unity and destroy the entity of the Algerian state."
Algeria, earlier in its conflict with Moslem fundamentalists, accused Iran of interfering in its internal affairs, and finally cut ties with Tehran in 1993.
Battling to get its oil and gas dependant economy back on course, Algeria announced on Monday it would sell off more state-owned companies, and has made clear it wants foreign investment for this.
